newsitem.title: UK: Sears backs chief executive Liam Strong.
newsitem.headline: Sears backs chief executive Liam Strong.

text.p: Troubled British retailer Sears denied it was not seeking a replacement for its chief executive Liam Strong, despite press reports that his job was offered and turned down by Next Plc chief executive David Jones.
"We have not employed any headhunters. The chairman and the board are strongly supportive of Liam Strong," said a spokeswoman at Sears. "We are not seeking a replacement for Liam".
Institutional investors are disgruntled with Sears, whose shares have underperformed the market by about 40 percent since Strong took the helm five years ago.

For some investors Strong's failure to deliver was illustrated by a profits warning issued two weeks ago, when Sears said its profits will fall well below last year's 100 million pounds level partly because of higher than expected losses at its shoe division.

Like-for-like sales at British Shoe Corporation, owner of Dolcis, Shoe Express and Shoe City, fell 2.8 percent in the six months to January 6. "We are just about at the end of our tether," said one small shareholder, who declined to be named. "It just seems like nothing goes right for them."
A spokeswoman for Philips and Drew Fund Management, Sears' single largest shareholder with over 12 percent of the stock, declined to comment on their view.
PDFM met Sears management last week for a regular update.

Although Sears sold its mail order business Freemans earlier this month to Littlewoods for 395 million, and pledged to return about 410 million in cash to shareholders in six months time, there are some investors calling for deeper changes.
They want to see a break up of the group to include a demerger of the very profitable Selfridges department store and the sale of the ailing British Shoe Corporation.
The company's other major shareholders include the Prudential, which holds about four percent, and M&G Investment Management with seven percent.
Analysts said there was unlikely to be any quick fix for Sears which makes running the company unattractive for most aspiring executives.
Strong, formerly marketing director at British Airways, was bought in in 1992 to transform the retail conglomerate.
